summary: The SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a public web application designed to make genuine NASA SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to everyone. Users can search for astronomical targets or enter coordinates to retrieve real Level 2 FITS data from the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive. The platform processes numerical layers and aligns observations using WCS data, allowing users to view a chronological timeline, blend images, and generate relative difference maps across different dates. We also integrated scientific quality checks, such as ePSF widths and spectral compatibility, to ensure scientifically responsible comparisons. Furthermore, we developed a supplementary prototype using C++, Python, and the Gemini API to demonstrate AI-assisted analysis. By transforming complex scientific data into an intuitive visual experience, this tool democratizes astronomy, empowering students and citizen scientists to explore the sky and investigate potential changes over time without falsely claiming new discoveries.
details:
Project Name: SPHEREx Sky Explorer

Website: https://cemberlitasmeninhack.com

Source Code: https://github.com/herenturker/spherex-nasa

1. What exactly does it do?

SPHEREx Sky Explorer is a public web application designed to make genuine NASA SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to everyone.

Users can search for astronomical objects, such as Barnard's Star, or enter custom Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates to explore specific regions of the sky. They can browse observations acquired on different dates, visualize them through an interactive timeline, and compare selected observations using side-by-side views, image blending, and relative difference maps.

The application highlights potentially interesting spatial and brightness differences without claiming that they represent confirmed astronomical discoveries.

2. How does it work?

Users select an astronomical target or enter RA/Dec coordinates and choose one of the available SPHEREx detector bands (D1–D6).

The application queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) through its Simple Image Access (SIA2) service to identify and retrieve genuine Level 2 FITS observations.

The retrieved FITS files are processed to extract numerical scientific layers, including IMAGE, ZODI, FLAGS, and VARIANCE. World Coordinate System (WCS) information is used to align observations onto a common celestial coordinate grid, allowing comparisons between corresponding sky positions rather than simply matching image pixels.

The interface organizes observations chronologically and allows users to select two observation dates (A and B). They can then visualize the observations using a fade-blending interface or inspect a relative B−A difference map.

The Sky Change Laboratory also provides scientific measurements and quality indicators, including spatial overlap, approximate spectral compatibility, valid-pixel coverage, and effective Point Spread Function (ePSF) width measurements.

These checks help identify potentially interesting differences while warning users when observations are unsuitable for reliable comparison. The resulting analysis is preliminary scientific screening, not a calibrated discovery or confirmation system.

Supplementary Analysis Prototype:

In addition to the main web application, our team has developed a separate experimental analysis interface using Streamlit. This supplementary tool incorporates a custom C++ engine for matrix manipulation and change detection, alongside a Python interface and Google Gemini API integration for AI-assisted interpretation of analysis results.

This prototype explores how conventional numerical processing and large language models can complement one another when examining image differences. Its outputs are intended to assist interpretation rather than replace scientific validation.

3. What benefits does it have?

Our project lowers the barrier to exploring authentic astronomical observations by transforming complex scientific archive data into an accessible visual experience.

Students and citizen scientists can investigate real infrared observations without having to manually navigate specialized astronomical archives or independently implement every data-processing step.

The chronological timeline, A/B comparison, blending interface, and preliminary difference maps provide intuitive ways to investigate changes across observation dates.

Scientific quality checks help prevent misleading comparisons caused by incompatible wavelengths, invalid pixels, coordinate misalignment, and instrumental effects.

Additionally, caching, retry mechanisms, and transparent processing logs improve reliability, reduce unnecessary repeated downloads, and allow users to understand what happens during data retrieval.

4. What do you hope to achieve?

Our primary goal is to bridge the gap between raw astronomical observations and public understanding.

We aim to provide an educational and scientifically responsible platform where people can explore genuine SPHEREx observations, investigate possible changes over time, and learn to distinguish astrophysical signals from observational artifacts.

We do not claim to announce new astronomical discoveries. Instead, we provide tools for preliminary investigation and help users understand which observations may deserve further scientific validation.

Future development of the main application could include more complete photometric analysis, spatially dependent PSF modelling, improved spectral calibration, and independent validation of potential detections.

As a separate long-term research direction, we are also interested in exploring whether similar numerical processing techniques could eventually assist spacecraft by filtering or prioritizing scientific data before transmission.

5. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The primary web application uses TypeScript and React (TSX) for its frontend, with Node.js handling server-side operations and scientific data processing.

PostgreSQL is used for persistent storage of astronomical targets, observation metadata, processed numerical layers, and data provenance.

The application is hosted on the Floot platform. Its primary data-processing and visualization workflows are implemented in TypeScript, including FITS handling, coordinate alignment, image comparison, and scientific reporting.

For the supplementary analysis prototype, we additionally developed a custom C++ engine for matrix manipulation and change detection, integrated through a Python and Streamlit interface. Google Gemini API provides AI-assisted interpretation of the analysis results.

Our development process also involved AI-assisted coding and debugging with ChatGPT. The astronomical measurements themselves originate from NASA/IPAC IRSA, not from generative AI.

Use of SI:

Yes. We used AI tools, including ChatGPT and Floot AI-assisted development capabilities, to support aspects of coding, debugging, and documentation. However, the project concept, system architecture, and scientific methodology were developed by the team. AI assistance was used as a development aid, not as a replacement for the underlying astronomical data or scientific measurements.

Primary Tools and Technologies:

- Astronomical data: NASA/IPAC IRSA

- Frontend: React, TypeScript, TSX

- Backend: Node.js, TypeScript

- Database: PostgreSQL

- Hosting and infrastructure: Floot

- Supplementary processing: C++, Python, Streamlit

- AI-assisted analysis: Google Gemini API

- Development assistance: ChatGPT

Supplementary Analysis Interface:

https://spherex-nasa-cemberlitas-men-in-hack.streamlit.app/
